text: Configuring a backup policy isn't the end of the job. This lesson covers why a backup that's never been test-restored is really just an unverified claim, a real and common failure pattern it causes, and what an actual restore-testing practice looks like.

Azure Backup and AWS Backup will both report a backup job as completed successfully for years. That status means the backup process ran without error — it does not mean the resulting backup can actually be restored into a working system. A backup can be incomplete or corrupted while the job keeps reporting success every single night, because nothing in that job checks whether a restore from it would actually work.

This is a genuinely common disaster-recovery failure: backups run faithfully for months, a real outage finally happens, someone goes to restore, and discovers at the worst possible moment that the backup is corrupted or stale even though the logs always said success. Now there's an outage and no working safety net, discovered at the same time, under pressure, with no time left to fix it properly.

A restore test means periodically restoring a backup into a real, usually non-production environment and verifying the result — does the system come up, is the data correct and current, does anything depend on a secret or configuration that never got captured. This needs a defined cadence, quarterly as a common baseline for a smaller environment, and again after any significant change to what's being backed up.

Teams reliably configure backups and watch them succeed, then skip proving a restore actually works, because that second half is ongoing discipline with no urgency until the day it's the only thing that matters. Treating restore testing as a recurring, scheduled task, the same way Chapter 4's monitoring alerts are recurring, is what turns having backups into having a backup you know works.
